title: Elissa: the flames of Dido's pyre
greek: moenia respiciens, quae iam infelicis Elissae conlucent flammis
short: Book V opens with the Trojans looking back at Carthage lit by the flames of Dido's pyre; Elissa is the queen's Phoenician name.
body: Elissa is Dido's original Tyrian name, the one used throughout Justin's account of the founding of Carthage (Justin 18.4-6). Virgil keeps it for moments of solemnity or intimacy: Aeneas swears he will never be sorry to remember Elissa (4.335, where Conington records the spelling Elissae of the best manuscripts), Dido calls on 'the gods of dying Elissa' in her curse (4.610), and here the narrator speaks of 'unhappy Elissa' as her funeral light reaches the fleet. Page notes that medium iter only means that Aeneas was well on his way, and that the winds shift through the opening of the book. The Trojans do not know why the blaze is lit, but guess from 'what a woman can do in madness' (notumque furens quid femina possit, 5.6), a last echo of Mercury's gibe (4.569-70). Book V thus begins, as Book IV did, with fire; and the book's own crisis will be another fire, the burning of the ships (5.659-99).

title: Eryx, Aeneas' half-brother, and Venus of Eryx
greek: fraterna Erycis litora
short: Eryx, a son of Venus and so Aeneas' half-brother, was the legendary king of the mountain in western Sicily crowned by the great temple of Venus Erycina.
body: In myth Eryx was a son of Venus and a famous boxer who challenged Hercules and was killed by him; Entellus recalls the fight, fought 'on this very beach', when he produces Eryx's gauntlets (5.410-14). The mountain in north-west Sicily that bore his name had a celebrated sanctuary of Venus. Conington notes that Dionysius of Halicarnassus cited its altar of Aphrodite Aineias as proof that Aeneas came to Sicily, and that Tacitus (Annals 4.43) records the people of Segesta asking Tiberius to restore the temple, recalling its origin; Page cites the same passage. Venus Erycina was also worshipped at Rome, with a temple on the Capitol vowed in 217 BC during the war with Hannibal. Aeneas founds the Sicilian temple at 5.759-60 ('a dwelling is founded to Venus the Idalian'), where Conington takes Idalia as an ordinary epithet. The family tie explains Palinurus' 'faithful shores of thy brother Eryx' and gives the Sicilian book its atmosphere of kinship and piety.

anchor: the yearly circle of the months
title: The anniversary of Anchises' death and the rites for the dead
greek: annuus exactis completur mensibus orbis
short: The games are held on the first anniversary of Anchises' death; Aeneas' rites anticipate the Roman cult of dead parents and the festival of the Parentalia.
body: Aeneas speaks on the anniversary itself (iamque dies adest, 5.49, as Conington explains), and his programme follows Roman practice for honouring dead parents: libations of wine, milk and blood at the tomb, scattered flowers, sacrifice and a feast, with games on the ninth day. Page explains the ninth day: there was a sacrifice nine days after a funeral (the novemdiale sacrificium), and Virgil's nine-day festival recalls it. The yearly rite foreshadows the Parentalia, the Roman festival of 13-21 February when families visited and honoured the tombs of their dead (Ovid, Fasti 2.533-70); Aeneas prays that he may repeat it 'in an established city and consecrated temple' (5.59-60). The setting makes the Sicilian book an exercise in pietas towards the dead, placed between the private disaster of Book IV and the journey to meet Anchises in Book VI. Homer's games for Patroclus (Iliad 23) are the literary model, but the motive has become filial and religious rather than heroic.

title: Myrtle, the plant of Venus
greek: velat materna tempora myrto
short: Aeneas wreathes his head with myrtle, the plant sacred to his mother Venus.
body: Page glosses materna as 'sacred to Venus', comparing Georgics 2.64, Paphiae myrtus, 'the myrtle of Paphos', Venus' city in Cyprus. The myrtle was Venus' plant in cult and poetry, associated with love and used in bridal wreaths, which gives the detail a quiet edge so soon after Book IV. It also fits the ritual, since worshippers wreathed their heads for sacrifice, and Aeneas has ordered everyone to 'twine your temples with boughs' (5.71). Myrtle has darker associations elsewhere in the poem. A myrtle thicket grows over the murdered Polydorus and bleeds when Aeneas pulls at it (3.22-40), and in the underworld those whom love destroyed hide 'shrouded in embosoming myrtle thickets' (6.443-4), so that Venus' plant overshadows Dido's place among the dead.

title: The snake: Genius of the place, or Anchises' attendant spirit
greek: incertus Geniumne loci famulumne parentis esse putet
short: The great snake that tastes the offerings is either the guardian spirit of the place or an attendant of Anchises' ghost; either way the dead accept the rites.
body: Romans believed that every place, person and family had a Genius, a protecting spirit, often pictured as a snake, as on the household shrines of Pompeii; Page quotes Papillon's note to this effect and adds that the famulus (Greek daimon), the attendant spirit of heroes, also took serpent form. Servius explains 'no place is without its genius', and offers several meanings for famulus: a slave buried with Anchises, as was once the custom at royal funerals; a minor power serving the deified Anchises, as Adonis serves Venus; or, after Pythagoras, a snake born from the marrow of the dead man's spine. Conington reports Servius' idea that the seven coils mean Aeneas' seven years of wandering, but doubts any special significance. The snake's harmless tasting of the food shows that the sacrifice is accepted, and Aeneas renews it with sheep, pigs and steers, the combination Page identifies with the Roman suovetaurilia. Its colours, compared to a rainbow, anticipate Iris later in the book.

anchor: First is the contest of rowing
title: The funeral games and the ship race
greek: prima pares ineunt gravibus certamina remis quattuor ex omni delectae classe carinae
short: Virgil's games follow Homer's for Patroclus in Iliad 23, but the chariot race becomes a ship race fit for wandering sailors.
body: Iliad 23 sets the pattern: prizes displayed, a chariot race, boxing, a foot race and archery, with quarrels, accidents, divine interference and generous judging. Conington notes that Virgil naturally substitutes a ship race, since his heroes had no chariots, while keeping his eye on the incidents of Homer's contest: a leader beaten through a helmsman's caution, a winner helped by a god after prayer, a crew limping home last. The turning post is a rock, like the meta round which chariots wheeled in a Roman circus, and Virgil himself compares the start to chariots bursting from the barriers (5.144-7). Page explains that each ship is named after its figurehead: Dragon (Pristis, a sea-monster), Chimaera, Centaur and Scylla. Aeneas acts throughout as a model president, generous and tactful, giving something to every competitor. Funeral games were also a Roman custom, which lets the episode join Homeric epic to contemporary ritual.

title: Trojan ancestors of Roman families: Memmii, Sergii, Cluentii
greek: Mnestheus, genus a quo nomine Memmi; Sergestus, domus tenet a quo Sergia nomen; Cloanthus, unde tibi, Romane Cluenti
short: Three of the four captains are made founders of Roman families: Mnestheus of the Memmii, Sergestus of the Sergii, Cloanthus of the Cluentii.
body: Claiming Trojan descent was fashionable among the Roman nobility; Conington notes that the practice was older than Virgil, since Varro had written a book On Trojan Families (De familiis Troianis). The links are made by etymological play: Mnestheus suggests Greek mnesthenai, 'to remember', as Memmius suggests Latin meminisse; Sergestus gives Sergius; Cloanthus gives Cluentius. Page remarks that the names chosen are curious: the best-known Memmius was the patron to whom Lucretius dedicated his poem, the most notorious Sergius was Catiline (L. Sergius Catilina), and the only Cluentius we know is the man Cicero defended in the Pro Cluentio. Whether any irony is intended is uncertain. Page compares Trojan ancestry at Rome to Norman descent in England. The device recurs with Atys, ancestor of the Atii (5.568-9), and with Nautes, ancestor of the Nautii (5.704), weaving the families of Virgil's Rome into the founding legend.

title: Simile: the rock-dove
greek: qualis spelunca subito commota columba... radit iter liquidum celeris neque commovet alas
short: After its burst of rowing Mnestheus' ship glides like a rock-dove that clatters out of its cave and then skims on motionless wings.
body: Page identifies the bird as the rock-pigeon, which nests in cliffs and is a remarkable flier, and points to the imitative rhythm of the Latin: the loud wing-claps (plausumque exterrita pennis dat tecto ingentem) followed by the smooth glide that 'stirs no pinion' (neque commovet alas). Apollonius, Argonautica 2.930-5, offers a comparable image of Argo gliding like a hawk on outspread wings. The simile catches both sound and motion: oars beating, then a hull running on its momentum. The bird returns in the archery contest, where a dove tied to a mast is the target (5.485-518): one arrow hits the mast, one cuts the cord and frees her, and Eurytion kills her in the sky. Doves are Venus' birds, and two of them later guide Aeneas to the golden bough (6.190-204); readers have seen a pattern of escape and death in a book of mourning, though such links are suggestions rather than certainties.

title: Portunus, god of harbours; Panopea and Phorcus
greek: et pater ipse manu magna Portunus euntem impulit
short: Cloanthus wins by prayer: the sea-nymphs and Portunus, the old Roman god of harbours, push his ship to the finish.
body: Portunus was an old Roman god of harbours (portus) and doors, with a temple near the river port of Rome and a festival, the Portunalia, on 17 August. Page and Conington both note his identification with the Greek sea-god Melicertes or Palaemon, son of Ino, who appears in Neptune's train at 5.823. Conington explains manu magna, 'with his mighty hand', as Homeric in feel, a god being larger than a hero, and suggests that the idea of a god pushing a ship comes from Apollonius, where Athena thrusts the Argo through the Clashing Rocks (Argonautica 2.598-600). Panopea is one of the Nereids, daughters of the sea-god Nereus, and Phorcus is an ancient sea-god. As in Homer's games, where Athena trips Ajax so that Odysseus wins (Iliad 23.768-83), divine favour, here earned by a vow, decides the result. Cloanthus' vow of a white bull, with the entrails thrown into the sea and wine poured on the waves, is the language of Roman ritual.

anchor: the kingly boy on leafy Ida
title: The cloak with Ganymede
greek: intextusque puer frondosa regius Ida... quem praepes ab Ida sublimem pedibus rapuit Iovis armiger uncis
short: The first prize is a cloak woven with the rape of Ganymede, the Trojan prince carried off by Jupiter's eagle.
body: Ganymede, son of Tros, was snatched from Mount Ida by Jupiter's eagle ('Jove's armour-bearer', because the eagle carries his thunderbolt) to become cup-bearer of the gods; Page recalls the earlier allusion at 1.28, where 'the honours of ravished Ganymede' are among the causes of Juno's anger. The description is a small ecphrasis, a verbal picture of a work of art, with movement in the woven figure (he seems keen and panting) and even sound in the barking hounds. The border of 'Meliboean purple' refers to Meliboea in Thessaly, famous for its dye (Page, citing Lucretius 2.500-1), and the 'double wave' of the border is a meander pattern. The subject is double-edged: Ganymede's elevation is a Trojan glory, but it is also a reminder of Juno's resentment, which will soon burn the ships. The aged guardians stretching their hands vainly upward anticipate the many figures in Book VI who reach out in vain.

title: Nisus and Euryalus
greek: Nisus et Euryalus primi, Euryalus forma insignis viridique iuventa, Nisus amore pio pueri
short: The two friends introduced in the foot race will die together in the night raid of Book IX; here their devotion is comic, there tragic.
body: Page calls them the Jonathan and David of Virgil's story. Nisus loves the younger, beautiful Euryalus 'with pious love' (amore pio), a phrase Page glosses as tender or pure affection; Virgil presents a Greek-style attachment in the language of loyalty. The race borrows from Homer: Nisus' fall in the blood and dung of the sacrificed steers copies the slip of the lesser Ajax in the cattle-dung in Iliad 23.773-7. From the ground Nisus trips Salius so that Euryalus wins. Aeneas' judgment, prizes for all, a lion-skin for Salius, a shield for the filthy Nisus, turns an obvious foul into a scene of good-humoured fellowship. The episode deliberately anticipates Book IX (9.176-449), where the pair make a night raid on the Rutulian camp; Euryalus is betrayed by a captured helmet glinting in the moonlight, and Nisus dies trying to save and avenge him. Read together, the episodes show how qualities applauded at the games, impetuous love that cheats for the beloved, become fatal in war.

title: The caestus: Eryx's boxing gauntlets
greek: duo... caestus, quibus acer Eryx in proelia suetus ferre manum
short: Entellus throws down the gauntlets of Eryx, seven ox-hides stiffened with lead and iron, still stained from Eryx's fight with Hercules.
body: The caestus was a boxing glove of rawhide thongs bound round hand and forearm; later Roman versions were weighted with metal, which made boxing far more dangerous than in Homer. Page notes that the 'seven huge ox-hides' recall the sevenfold shield of Ajax (Iliad 7.219-23), finds Virgil's exaggeration unnatural, and refers to the famous bronze statue of a seated boxer found in Rome, which shows such gloves. Eryx had worn these gauntlets against Hercules (Alcides) and been killed. The match reworks the boxing bout of Epeius and Euryalus in Iliad 23.653-99, and Dares' earlier victory over 'Butes, of Amycus' Bebrycian line' (5.372-3) points to a second model, the fight of Polydeuces with the Bebrycian king Amycus in Apollonius, Argonautica 2.1-97. Youthful speed is set against aged strength: Entellus falls 'like a hollow pine' but, stung by shame, rises and drives Dares across the ring, until Aeneas intervenes.

title: 'Yield to the god' (cede deo)
greek: non vires alias conversaque numina sentis? cede deo
short: Aeneas stops the fight before Entellus kills Dares: the strength is now another's and the gods have changed sides, so there is no shame in yielding.
body: Page translates 'seest thou not that strength alters and gods change? Yield to heaven', and argues that the words apply to both fighters: the gods have deserted one man and gone over to the other, so Dares may give in without disgrace, since he yields to a god and not to a man. Conington reviews the alternatives (Entellus' strength increased or replaced by divine power, or Dares' diminished), notes a supporting imitation in Valerius Flaccus, and prefers a general sense in which 'other strength' is the human counterpart of 'changed divinities'. Aeneas behaves as a president who prevents a death at funeral games, as the Achaeans halt the armed duel of Ajax and Diomedes in Iliad 23.822-5. The phrase also states a principle that runs through the poem: human effort succeeds or fails as the gods allow. Dares is led to the ships spitting blood and teeth, and receives the helmet and sword as consolation.

anchor: a better payment than Dares' death
title: Entellus' substitute sacrifice (meliorem animam pro morte Daretis)
greek: hanc tibi, Eryx, meliorem animam pro morte Daretis persolvo
short: Entellus kills the prize bull with one blow and offers its life to Eryx in place of Dares' death: a substitute sacrifice.
body: Page explains that the dead and deified Eryx is imagined as demanding a life, and the bull is sacrificed instead of Dares. The force of meliorem ('better') is disputed. Some, like Henry, hear the conqueror's brutal scoff, 'better than a coward like Dares', comparing Messapus' cry over a man killed at the altar (12.296). Page rejects this and prefers to understand that the life of a bull is a better offering than that of a man, citing Ovid, Fasti 6.162, where a pig is offered in place of a child. Conington reports Turnebus' explanation from a Greek formula used when a second victim was substituted for the first, and allows that some contempt for Dares may also be present. The vocabulary of anima pro morte and persolvo ('I pay in full') is the language of vows and substitution. The theme returns at the end of the book in Neptune's price for safe passage, 'one life shall be given for many' (5.815). Entellus then 'lays down his gloves and his art', retiring from the ring.

title: The omen of Acestes' burning arrow
greek: namque volans liquidis in nubibus arsit harundo signavitque viam flammis
short: Acestes' arrow catches fire in the sky and vanishes like a shooting star: an omen 'mighty in augural presage' whose meaning Virgil deliberately leaves unstated.
body: Old Acestes shoots last, when the dove is already dead, and his arrow blazes and vanishes. The narrator says that the outcome later taught its meaning and that seers in later days proclaimed the omen fulfilled (5.523-4), but he never says what it was. Page remarks that commentators have vexed themselves idly over it. It cannot be the burning of the ships later in this book, he argues, because the fulfilment is said to come late (sera); good guesses are the deification of Aeneas or of Julius Caesar, whose comet of 44 BC (the sidus Iulium) was taken as a sign of his apotheosis (Suetonius, Julius 88), while others think of some event touching Acestes or the Sicilians. Servius comments only on the words, noting that augurium suits a feathered arrow. Aeneas treats the sign as favourable, embraces Acestes and gives him first prize and a bowl that had belonged to Anchises, although Eurytion actually hit the bird. Eurytion, gracious, does not grudge it.

title: The Troy Game (lusus Troiae)
greek: Troiaque nunc pueri, Troianum dicitur agmen
short: The boys' cavalry display is the Lusus Troiae, a Roman ceremony often staged by Augustus, here given a legendary origin at Anchises' games.
body: The 'Troy game' was a parade and mock battle on horseback performed by boys of noble birth. Page notes that it was staged under Sulla, revived by Julius Caesar, and performed very often by Augustus (Suetonius, Augustus 43), and that Virgil 'invents for it a legendary pedigree' to please his patron: first shown in Sicily, then introduced at Alba Longa by Ascanius and handed down to Rome. Conington stresses that Virgil does not say Ascanius invented it, only that he introduced it into Italy, and that the show comes as a surprise outside the announced programme. Servius adds that Suetonius described its origin in a book on boys' games. Three squadrons of twelve riders, led by little Priam (son of Polites), Atys and Iulus, wheel and countermarch in figures that Virgil compares to the Cretan Labyrinth and to dolphins at play. Iulus rides the Sidonian horse that Dido gave him, a reminder of Carthage. The episode is the book's clearest bridge between Trojan legend and the ceremonial present of Augustan Rome.

title: Atys, ancestor of the Atii
greek: alter Atys, genus unde Atii duxere Latini, parvus Atys pueroque puer dilectus Iulo
short: Little Atys, beloved friend of Iulus, is made ancestor of the Atii, the family of Augustus' mother Atia.
body: Conington calls the line 'a compliment to Augustus, whose mother was an Atia', and sees in Atys' special friendship with Iulus a prefiguring of the union of the two houses. Page quotes Deuticke: Atia was the daughter of M. Atius Balbus and of Julia, the sister of Julius Caesar, so that the boys' affection anticipates the joining of the Atii and the Julii in Augustus himself. Conington adds that Atys has no other known connection with Troy, though the name occurs among the Alban kings in Livy (1.3), and that the Atii came from Aricia, which may explain the word Latini. Like the Memmii, Sergii and Cluentii earlier in the book, the line weaves contemporary Roman families into the legend. The repetition 'Atys... little Atys' (parvus Atys) is, as Page notes, an affectionate emphasis on the boy's youth.

title: Simile: the Cretan Labyrinth
greek: ut quondam Creta fertur Labyrinthus in alta parietibus textum caecis iter... inremeabilis error
short: The riders' intricate manoeuvres are compared to the Cretan Labyrinth, the maze Daedalus built for the Minotaur, which reappears on the temple doors at Cumae.
body: The Labyrinth at Cnossos was a building of 'blind walls' and a thousand doubtful ways, made by Daedalus to house the Minotaur. Conington reports Heyne's suggestion that Virgil would ideally have used the dance that Daedalus designed for Ariadne, which Homer compares to the dancers on Akhilleus' shield (Iliad 18.590-606), and chose the Labyrinth as the next thing that came to mind. The key word is error ('inremeabilis error', 'a wandering that cannot be retraced'), at once a maze-path and a straying. The image matters for the poem. Book VI opens with Daedalus' carvings of the Labyrinth on the doors of Apollo's temple at Cumae (6.24-30), and Aeneas' own wanderings are a kind of maze before he finds the way. The simile ends more lightly, with the boys likened to dolphins playing in the Carpathian and Libyan seas.

title: Iris as Beroe and the burning of the ships
greek: fit Beroe, Tmarii coniunx longaeva Dorycli
short: Juno sends Iris disguised as an old Trojan woman, Beroe, to persuade the weary mothers to burn the ships.
body: Iris, the rainbow, is Juno's messenger. Conington notes that the disguise copies Iliad 3.121-4, where Iris takes the form of Laodice to summon Helen, and that she lays aside her goddess's robe as Cupid laid aside his wings in Book I. Page explains the choice of Beroe, a woman who had once had 'birth and name and children': one who had seen better days might be expected to be discontented. Her speech plays on the women's exhaustion ('an Italy that flies us') and on a dream of Cassandra offering firebrands with the words 'Here seek your Troy'. Old Pyrgo, nurse of Priam's children, recognises a goddess by the eyes, the breath, the voice and the gait, standard signs of divinity, and Iris departs along her rainbow. The burning is a crisis for the whole enterprise: Ascanius gallops up and throws down his helmet, Aeneas prays to Jupiter, and a sudden storm quenches the fire, though four ships are lost. The disaster leads to the founding of Acesta for those who stay.

title: 'The seventh summer' (septima aestas): a problem of chronology
greek: septima post Troiae excidium iam vertitur aestas
short: Beroe dates the wanderings to 'the seventh summer' since Troy fell, exactly the phrase Dido used a year earlier: one of the Aeneid's unresolved inconsistencies.
body: In Book I Dido tells Aeneas that 'the seventh summer' is already carrying him over every land and sea (1.755-6). Since the Trojans then winter at Carthage (4.193) and a full year has now passed since Anchises' death (5.46), the same phrase here ought to be the eighth summer. Page's note on 1.755 shows that the chronology of the wanderings has long been debated. One might argue that the disguised goddess need not be precise, but the discrepancy is usually counted among the details Virgil might have adjusted had he lived to revise the poem, which he left unfinished at his death in 19 BC. The line is better read for its mood: 'pursuing all the while over the vast sea an Italy that flies us' (Italiam sequimur fugientem, 5.629). Conington connects this with Aeneas' own 'Italiam non sponte sequor' (4.361): the women express openly the weariness Aeneas keeps to himself.

title: Nautes, taught by Pallas
greek: tum senior Nautes, unum Tritonia Pallas quem docuit multaque insignem reddidit arte
short: Nautes, taught by Pallas to read the gods' anger and the order of fate, advises leaving the weary in Sicily; Roman tradition made him ancestor of the Nautii.
body: Tritonian Pallas is Minerva, named from Lake Triton in Libya near which she was said to have been born. Page explains Nautes' gift in terms of the poem's two supernatural forces: he can say 'what the gods' heavy anger portended' and 'what the order of fate demanded', the particular will of deities such as Juno and the general decree of destiny. Servius records that Nautes was said to have brought the Palladium, Minerva's image, from Troy to Rome, so that the Roman family of the Nautii kept the cult of Minerva, as Varro told in his work on Trojan families. Nautes' advice includes a famous Stoic-sounding maxim: 'whatever it shall be, fortune must be borne to be overcome' (superanda omnis fortuna ferendo est, 5.710). It is confirmed the same night by Anchises' apparition, which also tells Aeneas to seek him in the underworld with the Sibyl's guidance (5.722-40).

anchor: traces the town with the plough
title: Founding a city with the plough (urbem designat aratro)
greek: interea Aeneas urbem designat aratro
short: Aeneas founds Acesta (Segesta) by the Roman ritual of ploughing the line of the walls.
body: Servius, quoted by both Page and Conington, describes the founding rite as Cato had reported it in his Origines: the founders yoked a bull on the outer side and a cow on the inner, and with their togas girded in the Gabine manner held the plough so that the clods fell inward; the furrow marked the line of the walls, and the plough was lifted and carried where the gates would be. Conington adds that Varro gives the same account more briefly (De lingua Latina 5.143). Romulus was said to have founded Rome in this way. Conington compares the building of Carthage in Book I (1.418-38). The new city is named Acesta (Greek Egesta, later Segesta) after Acestes, who 'appoints a court and gathers his senators to give them statutes' (5.758), and the temple of Venus on Eryx and the priest and grove for Anchises' tomb complete the foundation. The scene is one of several in Book V where Aeneas performs Roman acts before Rome exists.

title: 'One life for many' (unum pro multis dabitur caput)
greek: unus erit tantum, amissum quem gurgite quaeres; unum pro multis dabitur caput
short: Neptune grants Venus safe passage for the fleet at the price of one life: the death of Palinurus that ends the book.
body: Neptune's promise has a condition: 'one only will there be whom you will seek, lost in the flood; one head shall be given for many'. Caput, 'head', means a life, as in a victim offered for others. Page compares Jonah 1.12 ('cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you') and the saying of the high priest in John 11.50 that one man should die for the people, parallels that bring out the idea of a scapegoat. Servius takes the 'one' as Palinurus, noting that strictly two men die, Misenus and Palinurus. The idea of substitution has already appeared in Entellus' bull offered 'in place of Dares' death' (5.483). The fulfilment follows at once: Sleep throws Palinurus overboard, and Aeneas mourns him without knowing of the bargain. In Book VI Palinurus insists that no god drowned him (6.348), so that the reader alone sees the cost of divine favour.

title: Sleep and Palinurus
greek: Phorbanti similis... ecce deus ramum Lethaeo rore madentem vique soporatum Stygia super utraque quassat tempora
short: The god Sleep, disguised as the sailor Phorbas, tempts the faithful helmsman, then drugs him with a bough dipped in Lethe and throws him overboard.
body: Page explains Phorbas as simply another sailor, and notes the rare diminutive loquellas ('soft little words', 5.842), borrowed from Lucretius' prayer to Venus, which gives Sleep's speech its coaxing tone. Palinurus' refusal is a model of professional vigilance: he will not trust 'deceitful breezes', clings to the tiller and keeps his eyes on the stars, so Sleep must use force, shaking over his temples a bough dripping with the dew of Lethe and the drowsy power of Styx. The fleet then passes the rocks of the Sirens (Odyssey 12.39-46), which Page places near the bay of Naples; Conington observes that Homer speaks of an island with a meadow of bones, and that Virgil rationalises the danger into reefs and drops the song. Aeneas takes the helm and laments that his friend will lie 'naked on an alien sand': Page and Servius explain nudus as 'unburied'. Servius adds that Virgil's executors Tucca and Varius chose to end Book V here.
